RENATO B. MARTINEZ renatobmartinez51@gmaiI.com Dear Atty. Martinez: This refers to your electronic mail dated 03 September 2024 seeking for guidance on whether or not an SB Secretary, who is a member of the bar, can practice law (e.g. notary public, execute legal documents, conducts of cases in court), At the onset we deem it prudent to highlight Section 7 of R.A. No. 6713, otherwise known as the "Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees" prohibits public officials and employees from engaging in certain acts or entering into transactions. Specifically, paragraph (b)(2) thereto prohibits the engagement in private practice of a profession. Such prohibition is grounded on the principle that public office is a public trust, and further serves to promote the observance and the efficient use of every moment of the prescribed office hours to serve the public. Be that as it may, the said prohibition admits of an exception provided that the following conditions are present: (I) such practice is authorized by the Constitution or the law; and (2) such practice will not conflict or tend to conflict with the public official or employee's official functions. Accordingly, for appointive officials such as the Secretary of the Sanggunian, Rule XII, Section 136 of the 2017 Omnibus Rules on Appointments and Other Human Resource Actions provides: "No officer or employee, whether in a permanent or regular capacity, temporary, casual, or hold-over, shall engage directly or indirectly in any private business or practice of profession. Exemptions may be allowed, subject to the limitations provided under R.A. No. 6713 and other special laws. Provided, further, that the following requirements/conditions are met: a. Written permission from the head of agency must be secured and renewed annually; b. Time devoted outside of office hours shall not impairin any way the efficiency of the officer or employee nor pose a "Matino, Mahusay at Maaasahan" Trunkline NO. (02) 8876 3454

conflict or tend to conflict with the official functions and must be fixed by the head of the agency; and c. Government facilities, equipment and supplies shall not be used while engaged in private business or practice of profession. Accordingly, appointive officials are not forbidden to practice their professions provided that, they should have secured prior permission or authorization from the head of their Department, as required by civil service regulations, and observe the limitations provided under the law. We hope to have sufficiently guided you on the matter. Very truly yours, B HORITY OF THE SECRETARY: ATTY J AN VICTOR R.
